text:
Recent evidence supports separating perceived relevance from factual support. A RecSys 2026 study found moderate ranking correlation between LLM and human explanation judgments, but low absolute agreement; neither reliably detected nonfactual content. Its recommendations include pretesting evaluation constructs and auditing factual accuracy. Thus, broad thematic similarity should not automatically count as specific personalization. [The Utility of LLMs in Recommender Systems Explanation Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01627)

For this task, a practical rubric adaptation is to annotate each recommendation–user claim as specifically supported, broadly similar, contradicted, or insufficient evidence. Record the supporting history item IDs, timestamps, title/description spans, or explicit feedback. Track unidentified items separately from relevance judgments; abstain on compatibility, ownership, unmet need, and current intent unless explicitly supported. Report specific-support and broad-similarity rates with clear denominators, alongside evidence coverage and abstention rates. These are proposed operational definitions, not a validated published scale. The 2025 position paper [From Noise to Nuance](https://aclanthology.org/2025.hcinlp-1.20/) supports pilot annotation, collecting reasons behind labels, and retaining meaningful divergent interpretations.

Use independent annotations before adjudication; preserve original labels and reasons. Report raw agreement and a suitable chance-corrected statistic, with disagreement broken down by rubric dimension. Agreement alone does not establish validity: a 2026 preprint found rubric clarification increased LLM-judge consensus without improving alignment with humans. For the twenty-user sample, report exploratory counts and cases by category; repeated recommendations do not create additional independent users or justify population claims. [Agreement Without Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13303)
